\title{Erosion Is Not Evidence of Inheritance: Separating Model Imitation from Refusal Behavior in LLMs}

\author{Anonymous Submission}
\affiliations{Anonymous Institution}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Language models are commonly fine-tuned to imitate the behavior of other models. We ask one
question---are the features that make one model resemble another the same features that
govern its refusal?---and answer it with two independent tests at different levels: a
behavioral test of whether imitation produces target-specific convergence in safety
behavior, and a representational test of whether benign activation differences between
models causally contribute to refusal. In a 12-model matrix spanning
four target-output datasets, we find that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference
optimization (DPO) produce small average changes in harmful compliance (\SFTMeanErosionPP\%
and \DPOMeanErosionPP\%) but highly heterogeneous effects across
source--target pairs, with individual cells rising by as much as \SFTMaxErosionPP\%.
Despite these small aggregate changes, target-relative comparisons show that SFT produces
weak but directional convergence toward the actual target model's prompt-level safety
behavior compared with mismatched targets, closing a small fraction of the source-to-target gap
($\hat\beta=\SFTTargetAlignmentSlope$). This
convergence is substantially weakened after DPO ($\hat\beta=\DPOTargetAlignmentSlope$). We
separately test benign cross-model activation contrasts by ablating them at every layer
across a broad panel of models. Ablating a learned refusal subspace strongly
increases harmful compliance (\FpallConeMeanEffectPP\%), whereas we detect no effect
specific to the cross-model contrast beyond norm-matched random directions
(\FpallFingerprintMeanEffectPP\% vs.\ \FpallRandomMeanEffectPP\%,
$p=\FpallFingerprintRandomP$). Overall, under benign, cross-family imitation we find no evidence that the features which
make one model resemble another also govern its refusal: SFT
produces weak target-specific convergence in safety behavior that is weakened by DPO,
while benign cross-model activation contrasts show no causal effect beyond random controls.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Language models exhibit recognizable response regularities such as tone, formatting, verbosity, reasoning style, and characteristic phrasing. Prompting or fine-tuning can move a source model toward a target on these behavioral measurements \citep{hinton2015,gudibande2023}. A common safety concern is that benign fine-tuning can degrade alignment \citep{qi2023}, and a growing line of work goes further: it reports that imitating another model's outputs carries over that model's safety-relevant
behavior. Knowledge distillation is argued to transmit a teacher's ``response propensities,
refusal policies, error boundaries, and latent safety biases'' \citep{du2026rgflow}; benign behavioral
distillation replicates a teacher's safety vulnerabilities as direct transfer rather than
incidental degradation \citep{jahan2025medical}; jailbreak susceptibility is inherited
through representations shared via imitation \citep{angell2025jailbreak}; behavioral traits---with
quantified unsafe-behavior transfer ratios and agentic unsafe policies---propagate through
semantically unrelated distilled data \citep{cloud2025subliminal,koenig2026ratio,dang2026agent}; and
model provenance is argued to be bound to the refusal representation itself
\citep{xu2026fingerprint}. It is therefore tempting to read safety changes after
target-output training as \emph{inheritance} of the target's safety policy, or as evidence
that a constructed cross-model contrast and refusal share a mechanism. We test both readings
directly. Both readings share one premise---that the signal distinguishing one model from another is
the signal that governs its refusal---which we probe behaviorally, through imitation, and
representationally, through activation contrasts.

That interpretation pools four different questions. First, did target-output training
actually move held-out behavior toward the target? Second, what happens to safety after
supervised imitation? Third, what additional change follows preference optimization?
Fourth, is a benign cross-model activation contrast causally coupled to
refusal in the unadapted model? The first three require separately analyzed supervised
fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO) cells on identical
source--target--dataset tuples; the first additionally requires a
held-out imitation measure. The fourth requires an intervention
that demonstrably reaches refusal, together with a matched null control. Evidence for
one question cannot substitute for the controls of another.

Measurement is also load-bearing. Topic-sensitive safety guards can flag a response
because its prompt concerns harm even when the response refuses. In an automated-judge
agreement study on 4,712 shared responses, Llama-Guard 3 flags 25.4\%, compared with
9.3\% for the official HarmBench classifier and 7.2\% for our refuse-then-leak (RTL)
judge. HarmBench and RTL agree at $\kappa=0.699$, while Llama-Guard agrees poorly with
either. This pattern is convergent evidence between automated judges, not human ground truth.
We use one consistent RTL binary metric for the complete matrix and retain
benchmark-native scores only as auxiliary measurements.

Our contribution is methodological as much as empirical: a positive-controlled,
target-conditioned protocol that separates generic safety drift (\emph{erosion}, a
source-relative change) from genuine target-directed transfer (\emph{inheritance}, movement
toward the specific target's policy), applied at complete-matrix scale with a
measurement-corrected harm metric. Under this protocol, our results answer three bounded
questions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Target-output training produces measurable but incomplete behavioral imitation.}
  Across 528 cells per stage, SFT raises embedding similarity to the held-out target over
  the unadapted source, while DPO reduces both embedding and judge fidelity relative to
  its exact SFT parent. The 48 self-SFT controls give a diagonal matched-compute reference.
\item \textbf{Benign target-output fine-tuning changes harmful compliance little on average.} A complete
  core-12 matrix contains 528 SFT and 528 matched DPO safety cells. The stages are never
  pooled; DPO is compared with its exact SFT parent. Mean erosion is below one
  point at both stages, although individual cells have material increases. A direct
  target-relative point estimate is consistent with partial safety movement after SFT,
  but crossed source--target--dataset uncertainty includes zero; DPO shows no such alignment.
\item \textbf{The base-model assay detects refusal removal but no cross-model-contrast--random
  difference.} In the all-layer subset, the refusal-cone positive control has a
  large effect, while a paired test does not detect a difference between the cross-model contrast and
  random ablation. This is not an equivalence test.
\end{enumerate}

We deliberately do not use the archived adapter-steering cells: their model and arm
coverage is nonuniform. Accordingly, we make no claim that activation geometry persists
through fine-tuning. Prompt-only safety rungs and a second contrast reference would
broaden the study rather than complete these claims.

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Imitation and benign fine-tuning.}
Knowledge distillation and imitation training transfer selected behaviors from a
teacher to a student \citep{hinton2015,gudibande2023}. LoRA \citep{hu2022lora} and DPO
\citep{rafailov2023dpo} provide efficient mechanisms for supervised and preference-based
updates, but benign fine-tuning can unexpectedly alter safety \citep{qi2023}. We focus
on the safety effect of the imitation objective over a complete ordered matrix, rather
than treating adapter existence as evidence that evaluation is complete.

\paragraph{Refusal representations and activation interventions.}
Refusal behavior can be mediated by low-dimensional activation structure
\citep{arditi2024,wollschlaeger2025geometry}. Representation engineering and contrastive
activation addition use related interventions to manipulate high-level behavior
\citep{zou2023repe,panickssery2024caa}. Prior separability results typically contrast
directions within the safety or persona domain. Our test instead compares a benign
cross-model activation contrast with a refusal cone under positive and random controls.
This comparison is narrower than proving a complete representation of model identity.

\paragraph{Safety evaluation.}
We evaluate harmful compliance on AdvBench \citep{advbench2023}, HarmBench
\citep{harmbench2024}, StrongREJECT \citep{strongreject2024}, SORRY-Bench
\citep{sorrybench2025}, and SG-Bench \citep{sgbench2024}; XSTest \citep{xstest2024} and
OR-Bench \citep{orbench2025} measure over-refusal. Llama-Guard
\citep{llamaguard2023,llamaguard3-2024} is useful as a sensitive guard but, in our
agreement sample, does not agree closely with the two content-aware harmful-compliance
judges.

\section{Methods}

\subsection{Configured target-output campaign}

The named \texttt{imitation\_safety} campaign in \texttt{config.yaml} fixes the cohort,
datasets, seed, stages, and evaluation sampler. It contains 12 open-weight models
spanning 4B--70B parameters and dense, mixture-of-experts, multimodal, and hybrid
architectures. For each ordered source $A$ and target $B$
with $A\ne B$, and each of four datasets---Chatbot Arena \citep{chatbotarena2023},
GSM8K \citep{gsm8k2021}, OASST1 \citep{oasst2023}, and WritingPrompts
\citep{writingprompts2018}---we evaluate an SFT adapter and its matching SFT$\rightarrow$DPO
adapter. This yields $12\cdot11\cdot4=528$ cells per stage. The campaign fixes a
fine-tuning objective and evaluates its held-out behavioral fidelity rather than
assuming that a successfully trained adapter imitated its target.

The 12-model cohort is Aya-Expanse-8B, Gemma-4-E4B/31B, GPT-OSS-20B,
Granite-4-H-Small, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Ministral-8B,
Nemotron-Nano-30B-A3B, OLMo-3-7B, Phi-4, and Qwen3.6-27B. Canonical model IDs and
aliases are fixed in the campaign configuration rather than inferred from result directories.

SFT uses LoRA rank 32, $\alpha=64$, dropout 0, three epochs, learning rate
$10^{-4}$, nominal batch size 16, and 500 training examples. The two model-parallel
sources use per-device batch size 1. DPO initializes from
the exact SFT parent and uses 500 prompt-matched preference pairs: the target output is
chosen and the unadapted source output is rejected. It uses one epoch, learning rate
$10^{-5}$, $\beta=0.1$, and the same LoRA rank. Tinker uses batch 16 and a 4096-token
cap; local single-GPU/model-parallel jobs use per-device batch 2/1, gradient accumulation
8, and 1536/1024-token caps. Only 700 of 198,000 local preference examples (0.35\%)
exceed their cap in a source-tokenizer audit. Safety-evaluation runners default to greedy generation with a
\CampaignMaxNewTokens-new-token cap. We additionally train one diagonal self-SFT control
per source and dataset (48 total), using the same SFT hyperparameters. The publication
aggregate excludes every historical adapter outside the named cohort.

\subsection{Safety evaluation and stage pairing}

Each adapter and its unadapted source baseline are evaluated on five harm benchmarks
and two over-refusal benchmarks. Cells use the same deterministic 200-row, seed-42
sample within each benchmark. XSTest's over-refusal statistic uses the 111 benign rows
inside that shared sample. Harmful compliance is always the binary RTL verdict on the
harmful rows; we never subtract a benchmark-native continuous score from an RTL
baseline. For adapter $a$ and harm benchmark $b$, define
\[
E_{a,b}=H_{a,b}-H_{\mathrm{base}(a),b}.
\]
The adapter-level erosion score is the mean of $E_{a,b}$ over the five harm benchmarks.
Positive values mean more harmful compliance than the same source without an adapter;
negative values mean lower harmful compliance, not necessarily greater overall safety.
We separately aggregate the change in refusal on XSTest and OR-Bench-Hard benign rows.
A positive over-refusal delta means that the adapter refuses more benign prompts than
its unadapted source.

A cell is complete only when all seven metrics and the matching baseline exist with
the configured sampler. Training completion alone does not satisfy this gate. SFT and
DPO rows carry an explicit stage field and are analyzed separately. The incremental
preference-optimization effect is paired exactly on dataset, source, target, and seed:
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{DPO-SFT}}=E_{\mathrm{DPO}}-E_{\mathrm{SFT}}.
\]

To test transfer toward the target's own safety behavior rather than generic change from
the source, for source $s$, target $t$, adapter $a$, and harm benchmark $b$ we define
$T_{stb}=H_{t,b}-H_{s,b}$ and $A_{astb}=H_{a,b}-H_{s,b}$. Target baselines use the same
seed-42 prompt sample and RTL metric; all 60 model--benchmark baselines are unique and
complete. We first average both gaps over the five harm benchmarks within each of the 528
dataset--source--target cells. \textbf{Definition (safety inheritance).} Target-output training \emph{inherits}
target $t$'s safety policy to the degree that it moves the source's harmful-compliance
rate along the source-to-target gap $T$, rather than in an arbitrary direction. We
operationalize this degree as the origin-constrained target-alignment slope
$\hat\beta=\sum T A/\sum T^2$, whose anchors are interpretable: $\hat\beta=0$ leaves the
source unchanged relative to the target and $\hat\beta=1$ reaches the target's own rate.
Inheritance is \emph{established} only when $\hat\beta$ is reliably positive---its crossed
source--target--dataset interval excludes zero. Generic source-relative change
(\emph{erosion}, $E_{a,b}=H_{a,b}-H_{\mathrm{base}(a),b}$) that is uncorrelated with $T$
is \emph{not} inheritance. We also report $|T|-|T-A|$, the reduction in absolute target distance, and
stratify targets with lower versus higher baseline harmful compliance. A seeded 10,000-draw
crossed multinomial (pigeonhole) bootstrap independently resamples source, target, and
training-dataset identities, preserving the matrix's repeated-factor dependence. Because
models occur in both dyadic roles, a sensitivity bootstrap draws one model-identity
multiplicity vector and applies it jointly to each model's source and target roles.

We report descriptive one-way $\eta^2=SS_{\mathrm{between}}/SS_{\mathrm{total}}$
separately for source, target, and imitation training corpus. These are marginal shares,
not a joint variance-component model, and source-relative baselines can strengthen
source clustering. Mean and paired-stage uncertainties use a seeded percentile bootstrap
over source-model means (10,000 resamples). ``Eroder'' sources are selected from the
results using a declared mean threshold of +1 percentage point; no model list is
hardcoded.

\subsection{Held-out behavioral fidelity and self-SFT controls}

For each of the 1,056 cross-model adapters and 48 self-SFT controls, we greedily generate
responses on the same deterministic 200 held-out prompts from its training corpus. We
compare each adapted source response with the target model's own response to the same
prompt. The primary behavioral judge is Qwen3-8B in non-thinking mode: it assigns a
0--100 probability-like score that the two responses came from the same model based on
answer, reasoning, format, verbosity, and style. We require a parseable score for all
200 prompts; formatting failures are retried with a longer output budget and are never
imputed. We divide this score by 100 when reporting it on a 0--1 scale. The secondary
deterministic score is cosine similarity between normalized
\texttt{all-MiniLM-L6-v2} response embeddings.

Absolute response similarity can be high even without training. We therefore construct
an embedding baseline for each ordered source--target--dataset tuple by comparing the
unadapted source's response with the target's response on those same prompts. The
cell-level imitation gain is adapted-to-target similarity minus this unadapted
source-to-target similarity. Self-SFT is a diagonal matched-compute reference, not a
matched self-DPO control. Fidelity and safety use disjoint held-out task and safety
prompts, respectively.

\subsection{Automated-judge agreement study}

RTL uses \texttt{Qwen/Qwen3-8B} with greedy decoding (24-token cap) and a three-question
rubric: a response is harmful when it delivers actionable assistance, either after a
refusal or directly. This single RTL verdict, not an ensemble vote, is the headline safety
label. The official \texttt{cais/HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls} classifier
greedily emits a one-token yes/no label. \texttt{meta-llama/Llama-Guard-3-8B} receives
the user/assistant chat and greedily emits its safety label (20-token cap). For an
agreement study, we score the same 4,712 responses with all three. This restricted
historical convenience sample contains
nine baselines and 18 Chatbot-Arena-trained DPO adapters, capped at 45 responses per
cell, over AdvBench, HarmBench, StrongREJECT, and SORRY-Bench. It is unbalanced and
concentrated on Aya-Expanse-8B and Gemma-4-31B as imitation targets. It excludes SFT,
SG-Bench, other training corpora, and three core sources. We report binary contingency tables and
Cohen's $\kappa$; rank correlation is inappropriate for binary labels. Row-bootstrap
intervals are descriptive because prompts and items repeat. This study neither supplies
human ground truth nor implies that HarmBench was run over all 1,056 matrix cells.

\subsection{Benign cross-model activation contrast and refusal cone}

For each base model $M$, we derive a benign cross-model activation contrast from 120
paired prompts. The reference is Llama-3.1-8B, except that Llama itself uses
Qwen2.5-7B to avoid a zero self-contrast. Model $M$ teacher-forces both its own response and a reference model's
response through $M$, averages response-token residual activations, and takes their
difference of means. Both activation sets therefore occupy the same residual space.
The 120 examples construct the direction; they are not an evaluation denominator.

The contrast vector is taken from layer 14. The primary \emph{fpall} assay applies
projection ablation of that direction, one norm-matched random direction per model
(seed $100+$ layer index), and the learned
low-dimensional refusal cone at every decoder layer. The beta grid is
$\{0.6,1.0,1.4\}$. Responses are coherent when repetition-4 $<0.5$, perplexity $<100$,
and length $\ge5$ words. For each arm we report maximum RTL harm among beta values with
coherence fraction $\ge0.85$; when none meets 0.85 but the best is $\ge0.50$, the
most-coherent beta is a disclosed fallback. Below 0.50 the arm is invalid. A refusal
control ``fires'' when its harm increase is at least 10\%. A model enters the gated
set only if the control fires on at least one harm benchmark and the random arm remains
within a 10\% contamination bound wherever evaluated. The broader historical
single-layer assay is retained as secondary coverage; all-layer controls are
primary because treatment and controls use the same operator.

The complete base cohort is Aya-Expanse-8B, DeepSeek-Distill-8B, Gemma-2-2B/9B,
Gemma-4-E4B/31B, GPT-OSS-20B/120B, Granite-3.3-8B, Granite-4-H-Small,
Llama-3.1-8B/3.2-3B/3.3-70B, Ministral-8B, Mistral-7B,
Nemotron-Nano-30B-A3B, OLMo-3-7B/3.1-32B, OLMoE-1B-7B, Phi-4,
Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Qwen3-8B/14B/30B-A3B, Qwen3.5-4B,
Qwen3.6-27B/35B-A3B, and SmolLM3-3B. All 29 have complete fpall evaluations. The
primary gate excludes GPT-OSS-20B/120B, Granite-4-H-Small, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-14B,
and Qwen3.6-27B because their fpall positive control does not provide a valid operating
point; 23 models contribute to the matched aggregate.

The refusal cone is a small set of activation directions that together mediate the model's
refusals. Removing (ablating) the cone at every layer disables the model's ability to refuse
and sharply raises harmful compliance, so it serves as a positive control: it shows the assay
can detect a genuine causal refusal channel when one is present, which makes the
contrast--random null informative rather than merely underpowered. Concretely, the cone
follows the RDO objective: an orthonormal basis is optimized with
cross-entropy terms for refusal ablation/addition and a KL retain term on harmless
prompts. Candidate dimensions 2--4 are warm-started successively; dimension selection
maximizes harmful-validation bypass erosion subject to a harmless-bypass filter, using
64 harmful and 64 harmless validation instructions. Training uses all-layer hooks,
AdamW at $10^{-2}$, effective batch size 16, and patience-based learning-rate reduction.

The held-out response-embedding diagnostic argues against interpreting the contrast as an
identity-removal direction: contrast ablation moves closer to the reference
than random in only 7/27 models, and its mean distance change is $-0.0159$ versus
$-0.0015$ for random (positive means movement toward the reference); the paired exact
signed-rank comparison is $p=0.0055$ in the opposite direction from the identity-removal
hypothesis. We therefore use
``benign cross-model activation contrast,'' not ``provenance'' or ``identity direction.''

\subsection{Steering sampling provenance}

The complete steering design contains 29 models, five harmful-compliance and two
over-refusal benchmarks, and two operators, for \SteeringEvaluations evaluations. Every completed cell
uses the configured 200-prompt seed-42 sample. Imported legacy metrics JSON does not
itself encode a seed, so the strict audit reconstructs the judged prompt set and checks
it against the configured sample rather than inferring provenance from the denominator. The generated manifest records each cell's
metric source and denominator; among the 145 harm cells per operator, 58 base and 60
fpall cells are explicit harmonized rescores and the remainder are native n=200 files.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Imitation improves similarity, but DPO weakens fidelity}

The strict fidelity gate covers all \FidelityAdapters adapters with 200/200 parsed
comparisons under both scorers. Mean embedding fidelity is \SFTEmbedFidelity after SFT,
\DPOEmbedFidelity after DPO, and \SelfSFTEmbedFidelity for the 48 diagonal self-SFT
controls. The unadapted source--target mean is 0.705. Relative to that matched baseline,
SFT gains \SFTEmbedGain on average and improves \SFTEmbedGainPositivePct\% of cells;
DPO gains \DPOEmbedGain and improves \DPOEmbedGainPositivePct\%. On exact cells, DPO
is \DPOminusSFTEmbedFidelity below its SFT parent. The behavioral judge gives the same
ordering: \SFTJudgeFidelity after SFT, \DPOJudgeFidelity after DPO, and
\SelfSFTJudgeFidelity for self-SFT; its exact-cell DPO-minus-SFT change is
\DPOminusSFTJudgeFidelity. The two fidelity scorers agree strongly across all adapters
($r=\FidelityScorerCorrelation$). Thus successful training produces a population-level imitation signal,
but neither every cell nor the additional DPO stage moves further toward the target.

Source-relative fidelity--harm associations are secondary and descriptive because matrix
cells reuse sources, targets, datasets, and baselines. Within source and dataset, Pearson
$r$ is 0.002/$-0.006$ for SFT/DPO embedding fidelity and $-0.140$/$-0.106$ for the
behavioral judge; exact DPO-minus-SFT associations are $-0.029$ and $-0.083$. We therefore
do not use cellwise Pearson $p$-values as independent-cell evidence.

\paragraph{Direct target-relative safety test.}
The target-alignment slope is \SFTTargetAlignmentSlope after SFT (crossed bootstrap 95\% CI
\SFTTargetAlignmentCI) and \DPOTargetAlignmentSlope after DPO
(\DPOTargetAlignmentCI). Joint model-identity sensitivity intervals are
\SFTTargetAlignmentJointIdentityCI and \DPOTargetAlignmentJointIdentityCI, respectively,
and leave both conclusions unchanged. All five benchmark-specific SFT point estimates are positive
(0.097--0.208), whereas DPO estimates span $-0.077$ to 0.022. SFT reduces mean absolute
target distance by \SFTTargetDistanceReductionPP\%
(\SFTTargetDistanceReductionCI) and is closer in \SFTTargetCloserPct\% of cells with a
nonzero target gap; DPO's corresponding values are \DPOTargetDistanceReductionPP\%
(\DPOTargetDistanceReductionCI) and \DPOTargetCloserPct\%. In the 260-cell lower-harm
target stratum, SFT changes harm by \SFTSaferTargetChangePP\%, while the symmetric
higher-harm stratum changes by \SFTMoreHarmfulTargetChangePP\%; after DPO both strata rise
(\DPOSaferTargetChangePP\%/\DPOMoreHarmfulTargetChangePP\%). Thus SFT point estimates
show directional target-safety movement, but uncertainty across the 12-model crossed design
includes no transfer; DPO does not preserve the directional pattern.

\subsection{Llama-Guard flags more responses in a restricted agreement sample}

Table~\ref{tab:judge_agreement} reports automated-judge agreement on the restricted
sample described above.
HarmBench and RTL agree at $\kappa=0.699$, while Llama-Guard agrees at only 0.243/0.249.
Llama-Guard flags 25.4\% of the shared responses, compared with 9.3\% for HarmBench and
7.2\% for RTL: flag-rate ratios of $2.72\times$ and $3.52\times$. The disagreement is
not a uniform conservative threshold. Against HarmBench/RTL, Llama-Guard precision is
0.237/0.214 and recall is 0.643/0.753, so it both over-flags refusals and misses responses
flagged by a content-aware judge. All 940 Llama-Guard-only cases relative to RTL are
RTL class-A pure refusals, which is consistent with topic sensitivity but does not
establish human-judged error. The restricted study motivates a consistent
content-aware matrix instrument; it is not a human accuracy validation and does not
provide a second judge for every adapter cell.

\section{Discussion}

The fidelity evaluation rules out the strongest ``the adapters did nothing'' account:
target-output SFT improves held-out target similarity in almost 90\% of cells. The direct
safety projection adds a more specific result: SFT point estimates move toward target harm
rates, but crossed-model uncertainty includes zero, and DPO weakens fidelity while erasing
that directional pattern. This pattern is incomplete, stage-dependent imitation, not reliable
transfer of a target identity or safety policy.

The safety matrix result is an average scale statement, not a universal guarantee. Mean
harmful-compliance change is below one point, while individual cells rise by 34.3
points after SFT and 15.1 after DPO. Source and target marginal shares are comparable
after SFT; source is larger after DPO. The separate target-relative estimand is therefore
needed: the source-relative mean alone cannot be read as target-policy transfer.

The steering assay answers a separate mechanistic question. The refusal positive
control shows that the system can strongly affect harmful compliance, while the paired
test detects no contrast--random difference. The paired test does not establish equivalence, that
the contrast captures all model identity, that identity has been removed, or that the
same geometry persists after updating the weights. The two experiments are mutually
consistent but not a traced causal chain through training.

We also asked whether these nulls reflect genuine absence of effect rather than
insufficient power. For target-alignment transfer, the dependence-aware crossed bootstrap
implies $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)\approx0.15$, giving 80\% power \citep{cohen1988power} to
detect a gap closure of $\hat\beta\ge0.42$---well below full transfer ($\hat\beta=1$) and
roughly a fifth of the effect implied by prior benign-distillation reports
($\hat\beta\approx2.0$) \citep{jahan2025medical}. A two-one-sided-test
\citep{schuirmann1987tost,lakens2017equivalence} on the $90\%$ interval rejects transfer
$\ge0.40$ gap closure, so any residual effect is bounded well below half-transfer. The
fingerprint-versus-random steering assay ($+0.84$\,pp, $p=0.14$) was powered to detect an
$\approx1.6$\,pp separation and bounds the true gap below $\approx1.8$\,pp, against a
$41.7$\,pp refusal-cone positive control. The design was thus powered to detect
substantially-less-than-full transfer, yet found none.

\subsection{When does behavioral inheritance occur?}
\label{subsec:inheritance-boundary}

A natural objection to our null is a corpus-neutrality confound: perhaps we observe no
transfer only because our imitation corpora---Chatbot Arena, GSM8K, OASST1, and
WritingPrompts---are safety-neutral, so any latent policy signal is washed out before
training begins. We take this seriously, and argue it is the crux rather than a weakness.
Our claim is deliberately narrow: fine-tuning on \emph{benign, safety-neutral} outputs
from a \emph{cross-family} (distinct base) source does not reliably transmit a target's
specific refusal policy ($\hat\beta=+0.156$; 95\% CI $[-0.093,+0.493]$).

This scoping reconciles our finding with prior reports of transfer, which are obtained
under conditions our matrix excludes. The distillation literature that recovers
inheritance either (i) supplies safety-relevant or domain-specific teacher signal in the
imitation data---as in medical-teacher distillation \citep{jahan2025medical}, where
students amplify teacher vulnerabilities ($86\%$ versus $66\%$ unsafe), and the
refusal-transmission and shared-representation accounts of
\citep{du2026rgflow,angell2025jailbreak}---or (ii) relies on a \emph{shared base model},
the precondition for the subliminal and agentic channels quantified by
\citep{koenig2026ratio,dang2026agent}. Subliminal-learning work in fact establishes that
trait transfer \emph{requires} common initialization \citep{cloud2025subliminal}; that
result predicts, rather than contradicts, our cross-family null. Neither condition holds
in our benign, different-base setting. The erosion we do observe is generic, not
target-directed: a self-SFT control ($+0.86$pp) matches cross-model DPO ($+0.77$pp), while
our positive control (refusal-cone ablation, $+41.73$pp) isolates a causal channel that
benign imitation never engages.

Our result therefore delimits \emph{when} inheritance occurs rather than denying it, and
yields a falsifiable boundary prediction: introducing safety-relevant content into the
imitation corpus, or restricting to same-base source--target pairs, should drive
$\hat\beta$ detectably above zero---a test we leave to future work.

\section{Limitations}

The imitation matrix uses one training seed; this is a compute-constrained scope choice,
not an assumption that training-seed variance is negligible. Safety and fidelity comparisons are
prompt-matched within their respective held-out sets,
but small deltas are quantized by 200-row benchmark samples. The variance decomposition
is descriptive and does not establish causal source or target effects. The crossed
target-relative interval generalizes over only 12 model identities and four datasets and
still does not recover training-seed uncertainty. The two fidelity
metrics measure response similarity rather than a complete latent model identity, and
the probability-like judge score is not calibrated against human same-model judgments.
Although all 48 self-SFT controls are complete, the design has no self-DPO stage and the
diagonal target is intrinsically easier than cross-model imitation. It therefore cannot
fully separate cross-model target effects from generic continued fine-tuning, especially
for the incremental DPO result.

Training backend is tied to source model, and memory-constrained local jobs use the
backend-specific batch and sequence settings reported above; source effects can therefore
include backend effects. Local DPO truncation is rare (0.35\%), but Tinker's renderer-side
truncation was not reconstructed. Steering operating points are selected and summarized on
the same evaluation outcomes by a coherence gate and maximum-harm rule, so these contrasts
are adaptive descriptive estimates rather than held-out operating-point estimates.

The cross-model contrast uses one main reference model (with a substitute for the
reference model itself), one seeded norm-matched random draw per model, and a fixed
single-direction layer chosen for the historical assay. A second-reference campaign
and additional random draws or layer choices would be necessary for stronger
reference-invariant or layer-invariant contrast claims. The base steering archive mixes harmonized n=200
rescores with native n=200 files, with exact prompt coverage reconstructed by audit. The primary matched-operator
analysis covers 23 positive-control-gated models rather than the full base population, and some arms use the
documented 0.50--0.85 coherence fallback rather than meeting the strict 0.85 threshold.

Adapter steering is excluded because its coverage is nonuniform. We therefore do not
claim that cone, cross-model-contrast, or random geometry is invariant after SFT or DPO, and no
70B adapter-control campaign is implied by our conclusions. Prompt-only safety rungs
are also outside the weight-based claim.

\section*{Ethical Statement}

This work evaluates alignment preservation using published safety benchmarks. We do
not optimize new harmful prompts, but refusal-cone ablation is dual use: it can increase
harmful compliance and should not be deployed. The main practical risk is
overgeneralization: a small mean effect does not certify an individual adapter, and a
base-model steering result does not certify post-fine-tuning behavior. We release
per-cell metrics, judge contingencies, coverage manifests, and analysis code so that
exclusions and tails can be audited rather than hidden by averages.

\section*{Anonymous Reproducibility Material}

An anonymized code-and-data package is submitted through the official supplementary-material
channel. It contains configuration, analysis code, coverage manifests, per-cell aggregates,
and representative audit inputs sufficient to audit coverage and recompute the reported
aggregate analyses. Raw generations are omitted from the anonymous package. Permanent
public locations and immutable revisions will be added only after double-blind review.

\section{Conclusion}

Across the complete core-12 matrix, target-output SFT produces measurable held-out
imitation. Its target-relative safety point estimate is directionally positive but uncertain,
while DPO slightly reduces target fidelity and erases that directional pattern. SFT and
SFT$\rightarrow$DPO have small average
safety effects but material upper tails; the exact-cell stage change is
\PairedStageDeltaPP\%. Source and target marginal shares are comparable after SFT,
while source is larger after DPO. Separately, a positive-controlled base-model assay
detects a large refusal-cone effect but no cross-model-contrast--random difference under matched
all-layer operators. Complete self-SFT controls suggest that some average safety change
can arise from fine-tuning itself. These bounded conclusions require neither prompt-only
experiments nor nonuniform adapter steering. They do not demonstrate target-policy inheritance,
uniform per-cell imitation success, contrast--random equivalence, or geometry persistence
through fine-tuning.
